title: ⭐⭐ Practice: two changes tied together, and the word that expects yes

questions.prompt: Complete: "The more books you borrow, ……… you have to carry home."

options.text: the heavier the bag
the more heavy the bag
the heaviest bag that
heavier the bag

questions.explanation: heavy is a short adjective, so its comparative is formed with -er, and the structure requires the in front of it: the heavier the bag. Using more with a short adjective doubles what the ending already does, which English never allows — more heavy is wrong for the same reason more big is. A superlative names the highest of a group and has nothing to compare here, since the sentence has only two things and they move together. And dropping the leaves the second half without the word that ties it to the first, which is what makes this structure a structure at all.

questions.prompt: In the shop a customer says: "Did you see some tall men with long beards?" Why is some used in a question here?

options.text: Because questions always take some in English.
Because the speaker already believes the men were there.
Because the noun men is countable and plural.
Because the verb see cannot be followed by any in a question.

questions.explanation: some appears in a question when the speaker expects the answer yes — here he is fairly sure the men passed and is asking for confirmation, which is why the ordinary any would sound colder and more open. Questions do not always take some; the usual choice is any, and this sentence is the exception the book prints to show that the rule is about expectation, not about grammar. Whether a noun is countable changes nothing, since both some and any work with countables and uncountables alike. And see combines perfectly well with any, as in did you see any tall men.

questions.prompt: Read this sentence from Lesson 24: "The drop in singles sales is the first casualty of a bitter battle for supremacy." What does casualty mean?

options.text: A victim.
A cause.
An accident that happens by chance.
A sudden and steep fall.

questions.explanation: A casualty is somebody or something harmed in a conflict or a disaster, and the metaphor of the sentence is military: there is a battle for supremacy, and the fall in sales is what it costs. Reading it as a cause reverses the sentence, since the battle causes the fall and not the other way round. The resemblance to the French word for chance is a trap of form: casual and casualty look related but only the first has anything to do with chance. And a sudden steep fall is what the verb plunge says elsewhere in the same text, which is why the two words are worth keeping apart.

questions.prompt: Which of these words does NOT belong in a library spidergram as your book fills it?

options.text: an atlas
a catalogue
a monograph
a supremacy

questions.explanation: supremacy is the position of being the strongest of all, and it belongs to Lesson 24, where the record companies fight for it — nothing about it names anything a library holds. An atlas is a book of maps and sits in the spidergram, as does a catalogue, the list of everything the library holds. A monograph is a book devoted to a single subject by one author, which is exactly the word the letter M in the diagram is waiting for. Three of these four come from the same page of the book; the fourth comes from a battle over pop records.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes: "There's hardly no paper left in the printer." What is wrong, and what should she write?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; the sentence is correct as it stands.
hardly is already negative, so the sentence needs any.
hardly should be replaced by scarcely to allow no.
no should be replaced by some, because printers hold paper.
hardly must be moved to the end of the sentence.

questions.explanation: hardly carries a negative meaning of its own, so adding no after it gives the sentence two negatives where it needs one: the correct form is there's hardly any paper left. Replacing hardly by scarcely changes nothing at all, since scarcely is negative in exactly the same way and takes any too. some is the wrong member of the pair after a negative, however full the printer may be, and the sentence is saying the opposite of full in any case. And moving hardly to the end leaves the double negative untouched while making the sentence harder to read.

questions.prompt: Dr Fox says the record companies have only themselves to blame, because almost every single released appears on a compilation album the same week. What is he accusing them of?

options.text: Of releasing too few singles each year.
Of refusing to put singles on compilations.
Of competing with their own singles.
Of raising the price of compilation albums.

questions.explanation: If the same song reaches the shops twice in one week, once alone at three pounds and once among forty tracks for a little more, the company is selling against itself — which is exactly the question Dr Fox asks about what a buyer would choose. Releasing too few singles is the opposite of what he describes, since his complaint is that almost every single is duplicated. Refusing to put singles on compilations is the reverse of the fact, and it is the reverse that would have protected the single. And nothing in the passage says prices went up; on the contrary, the album is presented as the cheap way to buy many songs at once.
